## Main idea

A limit describes what $f(x)$ approaches as $x$ approaches a particular value. The function need not be defined at that value.

The notation

$$
\lim_{x \to a} f(x)=L
$$

means that $f(x)$ approaches $L$ as $x$ approaches $a$.

## Worked example

Evaluate

$$
\lim_{x \to 2}\frac{x^2-4}{x-2}.
$$

Substituting $x=2$ gives the indeterminate form $0/0$, so we first simplify. For $x\ne2$,

$$
\begin{aligned}
\frac{x^2-4}{x-2}
&=\frac{(x-2)(x+2)}{x-2}\\
&=x+2.
\end{aligned}
$$

The two expressions agree for every $x$ near $2$, except at $2$ itself. Therefore,

$$
\boxed{\lim_{x \to 2}\frac{x^2-4}{x-2}
=\lim_{x \to 2}(x+2)=4.}
$$

::: {.callout-important title="A limit is not always a function value"}
The original expression is undefined at $x=2$. Its **limit** is still $4$ because a limit concerns values near the point.
:::

## Try it yourself

Evaluate

$$
\lim_{x \to 3}\frac{x^2-9}{x-3}.
$$

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Show solution"}
For $x\ne3$, factor the numerator and cancel:

$$
\frac{x^2-9}{x-3}
=\frac{(x-3)(x+3)}{x-3}
=x+3.
$$

Taking the limit gives $3+3=\boxed{6}$.
:::

## Takeaway

When substitution gives $0/0$, try simplifying the expression before evaluating the limit. Cancel a factor only where that factor is nonzero.
